children: Wall Street's fear gauge just posted its sharpest one-day drop in more than a year as investors moved quickly past the U.S. midterm elections.
The Cboe Volatility Index, or
VIX, plunged 20.26% to 16.61 on Wednesday
, its biggest one-day percentage decline since April 2025.
The move came as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, removing one of the market's biggest near-term political unknowns.
U.S. stocks rallied alongside the collapse in volatility. The
S&P 500 rose 1.6%, the Nasdaq gained 1.4%, and the Dow surged roughly 3%
, as investors bet that divided government could reduce the likelihood of abrupt policy shifts from Washington.
Lower oil prices also helped.

Crude fell sharply as investors increasingly wagered that the election result could put pressure on President Donald Trump to de-escalate the Iran conflict. That helped push Treasury yields lower and gave equities another tailwind.
But the decline in the VIX does not mean every risk disappeared.
Democratic control could bring tougher scrutiny of
AI data centers, energy companies, defense contractors and cryptocurrency
, while debt-ceiling fights and government shutdown risks remain potential sources of volatility.
The sector reaction already showed that distinction.

Large hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta gained, while data-center operators and semiconductor stocks came under pressure amid concerns that new infrastructure development could face tighter regulation.
Investor Takeaway
I think the VIX move matters because it shows investors were carrying a meaningful
political uncertainty premium
into the election.
Once the result became clear, that premium disappeared quickly.
A VIX at 16.61 is much closer to a normal risk environment than the elevated levels seen ahead of the vote, but it does not mean volatility is dead.
The market has simply moved from
election uncertainty to policy uncertainty
For investors, the key things to watch now are
Treasury yields, oil prices, AI regulation, fiscal negotiations and whether the VIX can stay below 20 once the initial post-election relief trade fades
The election removed one source of fear.
Wall Street now has to decide what replaces it.

title: Wall Street's Fear Gauge Just Made a Massive Move
